finding.claim: The /settings/email endpoint uses @login_optional instead of @login_required, so unauthenticated requests reach set_email with g.uid = None. Anonymous users can trigger the account-email change operation. The sibling /settings/password endpoint correctly uses @login_required, which suggests the wrong decorator was applied here. The email change is a likely account-takeover step, since the new address can then be used for password reset.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, which modifies a user's email

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid') (None if anonymous) and never aborts
set_email(g.uid, 'new@example.org') is called with None or whatever uid is in the session

finding.guards_checked: login_required (line 8) is not applied to this route. login_optional performs no abort or authorization check. The handler has no inline check of g.uid. I found no CSRF protection or other middleware in this file. set_email is a stub (line 48), so the impact depends on how it handles uid=None: it could update a row with a NULL user id or raise an error. The missing authentication check is a flaw regardless.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid and never aborts, and change_email (routes.py:36-38) has no inline check of g.uid. Only login_required (routes.py:8-16) aborts with 401, and it is not applied here.
verdict.reason: An anonymous POST to /settings/email passes through login_optional (routes.py:22) and reaches set_email(g.uid=None, ...) at routes.py:37 with no auth check. The account-takeover framing is overstated: an anonymous caller cannot choose a victim uid, and the email value is hardcoded. The missing-authentication flaw itself holds, while the impact depends on the stub set_email at routes.py:48.

verdict_facts.reason: routes.py:35 applies @login_optional, which only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") without aborting (routes.py:22). The handler at routes.py:37 calls set_email(g.uid, ...) with no check, so an anonymous POST reaches it, unlike /settings/password, which uses @login_required (routes.py:42). set_email is a stub (routes.py:48), so the real impact depends on how it handles uid=None.
